The PM should have included organizational change management (training, communication, incentives) within project scope and established adoption as a success metric from initiation
D. Neither is right — adoption rates typically improve naturally over 6 months and the assessment is too early
correct: C. Both have valid points from their frames of reference. However, PMBOK 7th Edition's value delivery perspective holds that a project is only successful if it realizes the intended business value. The PM should have included organizational change management (training, communication, incentives) within project scope and established adoption as a success metric from initiation
explanation: This tests understanding of PMBOK 7th Edition's shift from output delivery to value delivery. Technically both are partially right: the PM delivered specified deliverables (outputs); the business owner correctly identifies that outputs without adoption produce no value. The root cause: adoption was not included in project scope, success criteria did not include adoption rates, and organizational change management was absent. Professional PM practice in PMBOK 7th requires thinking beyond outputs to outcomes: if adoption was the business goal, the PM should have advocated for change management activities, user training, and adoption metrics as project success criteria from initiation. This is a lesson learned that changes how the NEXT project should be initiated.
source: PMBOK 7th Edition / Value Delivery / PMP ECO Domain III BE T2

question: A PM is managing a project with 8 weeks remaining and 3 team members who will each take 1 week of vacation at different times in the remaining schedule. Two of the vacations overlap with critical path activities. The PM is reviewing the resource management plan. What is the most complete risk mitigation approach?
options: A. Ask the two team members to postpone their vacations until after the project ends

B. Identify the specific critical path activities affected by each vacation, assess whether other team members can cover the work or activities can be rescheduled within available float, and prepare contingency plans for each overlap — then discuss the plans with the affected team members before making any schedule changes
C. Add buffer time to the schedule for all vacation periods to absorb any impact
D. Crash the schedule before the vacation weeks so critical path activities complete before the team members leave
correct: B. Identify the specific critical path activities affected by each vacation, assess whether other team members can cover the work or activities can be rescheduled within available float, and prepare contingency plans for each overlap — then discuss the plans with the affected team members before making any schedule changes
explanation: Team members' approved vacation time is a constraint that the PM should plan around, not override. The first step is analysis: which critical path activities specifically overlap with each vacation? Can those activities be rescheduled within the critical path's float? Can another team member provide coverage? The answers determine whether there's actually a risk or just a scheduling consideration. Only after understanding the full picture should the PM discuss options with the affected team members — and discussion should be collaborative, not directive. Asking people to cancel vacations without analysis first is both premature and will damage morale. Adding blanket buffer wastes schedule without targeted risk management.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Resource Management / Schedule Risk

question: A Scrum team has a new team member joining mid-project in Sprint 6. The existing team has high velocity and strong working relationships. The PM wants to integrate the new member without disrupting team performance. What approach best balances integration with performance preservation?
options: A. Have the new member work on isolated tasks for the first 2 sprints until they understand the codebase

B. Pair the new member with an experienced team member for Sprint 6, accept a temporary 10-15% velocity reduction as the cost of integration, set explicit integration goals for the new member, and include integration experience in Sprint 6 retrospective
C. Give the new member full sprint responsibilities immediately — sink or swim integration builds accountability
D. Protect the team's velocity by having the new member work on separate backlog items in parallel rather than integrating into the main sprint flow
correct: B. Pair the new member with an experienced team member for Sprint 6, accept a temporary 10-15% velocity reduction as the cost of integration, set explicit integration goals for the new member, and include integration experience in Sprint 6 retrospective
explanation: Research and Tuckman's model both confirm that adding a team member temporarily disrupts a high-performing team (Performing → mini Norming/Storming as the team adjusts). The most effective integration: (1) Pairing provides mentoring, knowledge transfer, and social integration simultaneously, (2) Acknowledging and planning for a temporary velocity reduction prevents the team from feeling 'behind' and the new member from feeling burdensome, (3) Explicit integration goals give the new member a success framework, (4) Retrospective reflection helps the whole team learn from the integration. Isolation delays full contribution. Sink-or-swim risks demotivation and errors. Parallel work prevents true team integration.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain I People T6 / Team Building / Tuckman Model

question: A PM is closing a multi-year project. During the final lessons learned session, a team member raises an issue that was never surfaced during the project: a process workaround that was used from Month 2 onward that effectively bypassed a quality checkpoint. The workaround produced acceptable quality but was undocumented. What should the PM do with this information?
options: A. Document it in the lessons learned but do not raise it further — the project is closing and quality was acceptable
B. Suppress the information — surfacing an undocumented quality bypass at close could create unnecessary audit risk

C. Document the workaround in lessons learned with context (why it was created, what quality checks were bypassed, what the actual quality outcomes were), assess whether the bypass created any undisclosed risk or compliance exposure, escalate to quality/compliance if material, and recommend the organization formalize effective workarounds rather than letting them remain hidden
D. Retroactively document the workaround as an approved process change
correct: C. Document the workaround in lessons learned with context (why it was created, what quality checks were bypassed, what the actual quality outcomes were), assess whether the bypass created any undisclosed risk or compliance exposure, escalate to quality/compliance if material, and recommend the organization formalize effective workarounds rather than letting them remain hidden
explanation: An undocumented quality bypass is an organizational learning and potential compliance issue regardless of project closure timing. The PM must: (1) Document it fully in lessons learned — suppressing organizational knowledge is professionally irresponsible, (2) Assess compliance exposure — in regulated industries, bypassed quality checkpoints may have regulatory implications, (3) Escalate if material compliance risk exists, (4) Recommend organizational improvement: the fact that an effective workaround emerged and remained hidden for 22 months indicates a gap in quality process management. Suppression is dishonest. Retroactive documentation of an unapproved change is falsification. Minimal documentation without impact assessment is incomplete.
source: PMI Code of Ethics / PMP ECO Domain II Process T17 / Lessons Learned

question: An organization has 5 projects competing for the same pool of 3 senior architects. A PM's project is highest priority per the portfolio ranking. The PMO director suggests the PM 'just grab the architects when they're free' rather than go through formal resource allocation. The PM needs 2 architects for 6 weeks. What is the appropriate response?
options: A. Follow the PMO director's suggestion — their guidance supersedes formal process in urgent situations

B. Use the formal resource allocation process regardless of the PMO director's suggestion, ensuring the request is documented, processed through portfolio management, and that impacted projects receive proper visibility into the allocation decision
C. Informally secure the architects first, then formalize the allocation retroactively
D. Accept whatever architects are available informally and supplement with external contractors through procurement
correct: B. Use the formal resource allocation process regardless of the PMO director's suggestion, ensuring the request is documented, processed through portfolio management, and that impacted projects receive proper visibility into the allocation decision
explanation: Informal resource 'grabbing' — even when encouraged by the PMO director — creates several organizational problems: (1) Other project PMs cannot plan accurately if resource allocation is unpredictable and undocumented, (2) The portfolio management process loses its effectiveness if exceptions routinely bypass it, (3) There is no accountability trail if the allocation creates downstream problems. The PM's project being highest priority is a justification for formal allocation — not for bypassing the process. Using priority status through formal channels is appropriate and will likely result in the PM getting the architects. The formal process protects everyone, including the PM.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain III BE / Portfolio Governance / Resource Management

question: A project using hybrid methodology has the following situation: the agile delivery team has completed 18 of 22 planned epics. The remaining 4 epics cannot be delivered before the fixed contract end date based on current velocity. The customer has a strict contractual deadline. The PM must recommend a path forward. What options should be presented?
options: A. Request a contract extension — the only acceptable outcome is delivering all 22 epics

B. Present the customer with three options with full analysis: (1) Reduce scope to the 18 completed epics — end on time as contracted; (2) Prioritize the 4 remaining epics and accelerate (crash/additional team capacity) to attempt delivery — quantify cost and residual risk; (3) Formally extend the contract for the remaining 4 epics — with timeline and cost impact
C. Deliver the 18 completed epics by the deadline and include partially completed epics where possible
D. Absorb the remaining 4 epics into the current velocity and accept a quality reduction to meet the deadline
correct: B. Present the customer with three options with full analysis: (1) Reduce scope to the 18 completed epics — end on time as contracted; (2) Prioritize the 4 remaining epics and accelerate (crash/additional team capacity) to attempt delivery — quantify cost and residual risk; (3) Formally extend the contract for the remaining 4 epics — with timeline and cost impact
explanation: A contractual situation with a scope gap requires transparent, options-based communication — not unilateral decisions. The PM must present all viable options with full impact analysis: scope reduction (clean, on-time delivery of 18 epics, contract technically delivered on time if those 18 represented the committed scope), acceleration (can the 4 remaining be crashed? at what cost? with what risk?), and extension (formal contract amendment — what does it cost and how long?). The customer must make this decision with full information. Delivering partially completed epics risks quality and may not meet the DoD. Reducing quality to hit the deadline is never an acceptable option — it merely defers the rework cost.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Hybrid / Contract Management / Scope

question: A PM notices that during online meetings, the same 3 team members (all from the same geographic location) dominate discussions, while 6 others (spread across other locations) rarely contribute verbally. Post-meeting surveys show that the quieter group has relevant insights they don't share. The PM suspects this is partly a technology issue (audio quality) and partly a facilitation issue. What structural changes would most effectively address this?
options: A. Address the audio quality issue first and then monitor whether participation naturally increases
B. Implement a round-robin speaking format — give everyone equal mandatory speaking time

C. Combine technical and facilitation interventions: upgrade audio infrastructure for affected locations, use structured participation formats (e.g., 1-2-4-All, written round before verbal), rotate facilitation responsibilities, implement explicit 'voice the room' check-ins mid-meeting, and collect post-meeting input channels for those who didn't speak
D. Split into smaller geographic-based sub-meetings and consolidate key decisions in a brief plenary
correct: C. Combine technical and facilitation interventions: upgrade audio infrastructure for affected locations, use structured participation formats (e.g., 1-2-4-All, written round before verbal), rotate facilitation responsibilities, implement explicit 'voice the room' check-ins mid-meeting, and collect post-meeting input channels for those who didn't speak
explanation: The PM correctly identifies a multi-factor problem: technical (audio quality creates frustration and hesitation to speak) and facilitation (unstructured formats favor naturally dominant participants and those for whom verbal interruption is culturally comfortable). A single intervention addresses only one factor. The combined approach addresses both: technical fix removes friction, structured formats level the participation field regardless of personality or culture, rotating facilitation builds all participants' skills, and async channels capture insights from those who won't speak verbally. Round-robin mandatory speaking can feel coercive and produce low-quality contributions. Geographic sub-meetings fragment team cohesion without solving the participation pattern.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain I People T11 / Virtual Teams / Meeting Facilitation

question: A PM is midway through a predictive project when a stakeholder requests a change to a deliverable that has already passed quality control and been formally accepted. The change is strategically valuable but requires rework of the accepted deliverable. How should the PM handle this?
options: A. Refuse the change — formally accepted deliverables cannot be modified
B. Make the change immediately since the stakeholder has legitimate business reasons

C. Process a formal change request: assess impact on all affected deliverables, cost, schedule, and quality; present the analysis including any previously accepted deliverables that must be re-opened; obtain CCB approval; update all affected documentation and restart QC on modified deliverables
D. Make the change and update the project documents without going through the CCB since the scope was previously accepted
correct: C. Process a formal change request: assess impact on all affected deliverables, cost, schedule, and quality; present the analysis including any previously accepted deliverables that must be re-opened; obtain CCB approval; update all affected documentation and restart QC on modified deliverables
explanation: Formal acceptance does not freeze deliverables permanently — changes are possible but must go through integrated change control regardless of acceptance status. The change request process is especially important here because: (1) rework of an accepted deliverable may affect other deliverables that depended on its original form, (2) QC must be repeated on modified work, (3) the cost/schedule impact may be significant and requires explicit authorization. Making the change without CCB approval bypasses governance for what could be a material scope and cost change. Refusing the change without analysis may sacrifice legitimate strategic value. The formal process ensures the organization makes an informed decision.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Integrated Change Control / Validate Scope

question: A PM is working on a project in a Balanced Matrix organization. The project is 60% complete and the functional manager withdraws a key developer citing a critical operational emergency, promising to return them in 2 weeks. The PM has no authority to override this. Three weeks later, the developer has not returned. What should the PM do?
options: A. Continue waiting — functional managers have authority in matrix organizations and the PM must respect that
B. Immediately escalate to HR since the functional manager broke their commitment

C. Formally document the 3-week absence and its schedule impact, escalate to the PM's sponsor with specific data (activities delayed, float consumed, projected delay to project end), and request organizational intervention to either return the resource or provide an equivalent replacement — treating this as an active project issue, not a scheduling inconvenience
D. Hire a contract developer through procurement to replace the function permanently
correct: C. Formally document the 3-week absence and its schedule impact, escalate to the PM's sponsor with specific data (activities delayed, float consumed, projected delay to project end), and request organizational intervention to either return the resource or provide an equivalent replacement — treating this as an active project issue, not a scheduling inconvenience
explanation: Three weeks versus a promised 2 weeks is a broken commitment with measurable project impact. At 60% complete, a critical developer's extended absence likely affects the critical path. The PM's appropriate response in a balanced matrix: (1) Quantify the real schedule impact (not just the inconvenience), (2) Escalate to sponsor with data — this is an organizational-level resource conflict requiring arbitration above the PM's authority, (3) Request specific resolution (return of the developer or equivalent replacement), not just 'acknowledgment.' Continued waiting is passive and allows the situation to compound. HR escalation is inappropriate for a resource conflict that hasn't yet been addressed organizationally. Procurement is potentially valid but expensive and slow — should be a fallback after organizational escalation.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain III BE / Matrix Organization / Resource Escalation

question: A PM is reviewing a quality management plan. The plan specifies that all deliverables will be tested by the project team before customer acceptance. A quality auditor notes that having the same team test what they built is a significant quality risk. The PM believes the team is professional and objective. Who is making the correct point, and what should be done?
options: A. The PM is correct — professionals can objectively test their own work

B. The auditor is correct — self-testing creates confirmation bias regardless of professionalism. The plan should include independent verification: a separate QA team, peer review from outside the development team, or customer involvement in functional testing before formal acceptance
C. Both are partially right — self-testing is sufficient for lower-risk deliverables but independent testing is needed for critical ones
D. The issue is moot — professional teams should always be trusted to ensure quality
correct: B. The auditor is correct — self-testing creates confirmation bias regardless of professionalism. The plan should include independent verification: a separate QA team, peer review from outside the development team, or customer involvement in functional testing before formal acceptance
explanation: The auditor's concern is supported by established quality management research: developers testing their own work consistently find fewer defects than independent testers — not due to lack of professionalism but due to confirmation bias (testing what you intended to build, not what might be wrong), familiarity blindness (not seeing obvious errors in familiar code), and unconscious assumptions about how features should work. Independent testing is a fundamental quality principle precisely because professionalism cannot overcome cognitive bias. The plan should be revised to include independent verification proportional to deliverable risk. Option C is closest to correct but understates the systematic nature of the bias.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process T7 / Quality Management / Independent Testing

question: A PM has been leading a project for 14 months. The team is in the Performing stage. The PM receives a significant promotion and will be replaced by a new PM in 2 weeks. What is the outgoing PM's responsibility to the team and the incoming PM?
options: A. Complete the handover documentation and step aside — the incoming PM will quickly adapt to the team

B. Execute a comprehensive knowledge transfer: document team dynamics, individual strengths and development areas, stakeholder relationships and sensitivities, informal team norms, decisions made and their rationale, technical context, and provide introduction meetings between the incoming PM and all key stakeholders and team members
C. Inform the team about the change and allow them to self-organize — Performing-stage teams don't need management continuity
D. Recommend that the incoming PM maintain identical management practices for at least 3 months to avoid disrupting the high-performing team
correct: B. Execute a comprehensive knowledge transfer: document team dynamics, individual strengths and development areas, stakeholder relationships and sensitivities, informal team norms, decisions made and their rationale, technical context, and provide introduction meetings between the incoming PM and all key stakeholders and team members
explanation: A PM transition on a high-performing team is a significant risk — Performing-stage teams can regress to Norming or Storming if not managed carefully. The outgoing PM's responsibility is comprehensive knowledge transfer that goes beyond project documentation: relationship context (how each stakeholder prefers to engage), team dynamics (who are the informal leaders, what sensitivities exist), decision history (why past decisions were made — prevents the incoming PM from re-opening settled issues), and warm introductions that lend the outgoing PM's relationship credibility to the incoming PM. Recommending identical practices ignores that the incoming PM has their own legitimate style — the goal is continuity of relationships and context, not cloning behavior.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain I People T6 / Team Continuity / Leadership Transition

question: During Sprint Planning, a developer identifies a technical dependency that wasn't known during backlog refinement: the selected user story requires a third-party API that is deprecated and will be shut down in 45 days. The story is high-priority and completing it with the current API would waste the work. How should the team handle this?
options: A. Proceed with the current API — 45 days is enough time to complete the story and the technical debt can be addressed later
B. Remove the story from the sprint — technical dependencies that emerge during planning should exclude stories from the sprint

C. During sprint planning, openly discuss the constraint: options include (1) defer the story and spike the alternative API in this sprint (time-boxed research task), (2) split the story — build with current API as an MVP knowing migration will be needed, (3) accept the story and build directly against the replacement API if it's production-ready. The team and PO decide based on risk tolerance and value priority
D. Escalate immediately to the sponsor since a third-party dependency risk is above the team's authority
correct: C. During sprint planning, openly discuss the constraint: options include (1) defer the story and spike the alternative API in this sprint (time-boxed research task), (2) split the story — build with current API as an MVP knowing migration will be needed, (3) accept the story and build directly against the replacement API if it's production-ready. The team and PO decide based on risk tolerance and value priority
explanation: This is exactly the type of constraint that emerges during Sprint Planning and must be resolved transparently before the team commits. An API shutting down in 45 days is not an ignorable technical detail — it fundamentally changes the story's design. The team should explore all options: (1) A spike (technical investigation story) to assess alternative APIs — yields information for next sprint, (2) Build with deprecated API accepting a known migration in the next sprint (deliberate technical debt), (3) Build directly against the replacement if it's stable. The Product Owner must participate in this decision since it affects value delivery timing. Removing stories without exploration destroys value. Escalating a team-level technical decision to the sponsor is inappropriate.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Sprint Planning / Technical Risk

question: A PM has been asked to manage a project that a colleague declined, citing 'impossible scope, unrealistic timeline, and insufficient budget.' The PM has reviewed the project and agrees with the assessment. The sponsor insists the project will proceed as planned. What should the PM do?
options: A. Accept the project — sponsors have authority and the PM must manage within the given constraints
B. Decline the project as the previous PM did — taking on an impossible project is professionally risky

C. Accept the project conditionally: conduct a rapid formal assessment of scope, timeline, and budget feasibility; present the findings to the sponsor with specific data; propose what is achievable within the current constraints and what would need to change (scope reduction, timeline extension, or budget increase) to achieve the full objective — making acceptance of the assignment contingent on honest stakeholder expectations
D. Accept the project and immediately begin escalating the constraint issues through the PMO
correct: C. Accept the project conditionally: conduct a rapid formal assessment of scope, timeline, and budget feasibility; present the findings to the sponsor with specific data; propose what is achievable within the current constraints and what would need to change (scope reduction, timeline extension, or budget increase) to achieve the full objective — making acceptance of the assignment contingent on honest stakeholder expectations
explanation: A PM who accepts a project known to be infeasible as defined — without surfacing that infeasibility — is setting up the project for failure and themselves for accountability without authority. The professional response: (1) Accept the challenge of the assessment (not blind acceptance of impossible constraints), (2) Conduct a rapid but rigorous feasibility analysis with specific data, (3) Present findings professionally — not as a refusal but as a contribution: 'Here's what's achievable within these constraints, and here's what adjusting X, Y, or Z would enable,' (4) Require honest stakeholder expectations before committing. This demonstrates professional integrity while demonstrating value. Blind acceptance is professionally negligent. Outright refusal without contributing analysis abandons professional responsibility.
source: PMI Code of Ethics / PMP ECO Domain III BE / Project Initiation

question: A PM is developing the Communications Management Plan. The project has 12 stakeholders. Using the communication channels formula, how many channels exist, and what does this imply for the plan?
options: A. 66 channels — the PM must manage every channel individually in the plan

B. 66 channels — this volume justifies a structured communication plan that uses stakeholder groups, push/pull channels, and information hierarchy to manage complexity rather than attempting individual management of all channels
C. 132 channels — bidirectional communication doubles the one-way channel count
D. 12 channels — each stakeholder is one channel to manage
correct: B. 66 channels — this volume justifies a structured communication plan that uses stakeholder groups, pull/pull channels, and information hierarchy to manage complexity rather than attempting individual management of all channels
explanation: n(n-1)/2 = 12(11)/2 = 66 channels. This formula counts unique pairs — the pathways through which information can flow. 66 channels for 12 stakeholders is the insight that justifies structured communication planning: if the PM tried to manage every channel individually, the overhead would consume more time than the project work itself. The plan must therefore use: information architecture (who needs what level of detail), push channels (reports, emails sent to groups), pull channels (dashboards stakeholders access on demand), and tiered communication frequencies. The implication of 66 channels is not 'manage each individually' but rather 'this complexity requires disciplined structure.'
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process T2 / Communications Management

question: A PM receives competing urgent requests from two equally high-priority stakeholders at the same time, each claiming their request is most critical and should be addressed first. Both requests are outside the PM's current project scope. What is the BEST response?
options: A. Address the request from the stakeholder with more organizational power first
B. Handle whichever request came first — first-in-first-out is the most defensible approach

C. Acknowledge both stakeholders, explain you are evaluating two concurrent urgent requests, establish objective criteria to prioritize (business impact, time-sensitivity, dependency chain, alignment with project objectives), make a transparent decision, and communicate the rationale to both stakeholders simultaneously
D. Escalate both requests to the sponsor to avoid having to make a prioritization decision
correct: C. Acknowledge both stakeholders, explain you are evaluating two concurrent urgent requests, establish objective criteria to prioritize (business impact, time-sensitivity, dependency chain, alignment with project objectives), make a transparent decision, and communicate the rationale to both stakeholders simultaneously
explanation: Competing urgent requests from equal-authority stakeholders require: (1) Acknowledgment that prevents both from feeling ignored, (2) Objective criteria for prioritization — not power, not arrival order, not gut feeling, (3) A transparent decision communicated to both simultaneously, not sequentially. Stakeholder A should not hear they are deprioritized from Stakeholder B's reaction. Both requests are also outside project scope — which may mean they should be logged as change requests or routed to a different resource entirely. Prioritizing by power is politically expedient but undermines integrity. FIFO ignores the substantive difference in urgency. Escalating both without attempting objective analysis is avoiding the PM's responsibility.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain I People T9 / Stakeholder Management / Decision-Making

question: A project's risk management plan specifies monthly risk reviews. In Month 4, during execution, a team member identifies a new risk that has a 70% probability of occurring within the next 10 days and a $200,000 impact. The next scheduled risk review is in 3 weeks. What should happen?
options: A. Log the risk in the risk register and review it at the scheduled monthly meeting

B. Immediately assess and respond to the risk without waiting for the next scheduled review — the risk management plan's monthly cadence is a minimum frequency, not a prohibition on interim action for urgent risks
C. Ask the team member to monitor the risk and report if it materializes before the next review
D. Update the risk register and send an email notification to the risk owner — this fulfills the process obligation
correct: B. Immediately assess and respond to the risk without waiting for the next scheduled review — the risk management plan's monthly cadence is a minimum frequency, not a prohibition on interim action for urgent risks
explanation: Risk management plans define minimum monitoring cadences — they do not prohibit urgent action when a high-probability, high-impact, time-sensitive risk is identified. A 70% probability risk materializing within 10 days requires immediate response: (1) Verify the probability and impact assessment, (2) Implement an immediate risk response (avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept with contingency), (3) Update the risk register, (4) Notify relevant stakeholders. Waiting 3 weeks for a risk with 70% probability of occurring in 10 days means the risk will almost certainly materialize before action is taken — at $200K impact. Process adherence should enable good decisions, not prevent them.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process T3 / Monitor Risks / Risk Response Urgency

question: A PM is asked to join a project already 30% complete that has: no formal project charter, no approved scope statement, no schedule baseline, and a team that has been working from informal verbal agreements with the sponsor. The sponsor says all this 'paperwork' is unnecessary for a small team. What should the PM do in the first week?
options: A. Adopt the sponsor's approach — if the team has worked successfully without documentation, adding it now creates disruption
B. Immediately create all missing documents using the existing team's tribal knowledge as input, get everything signed off by the sponsor, and establish formal governance going forward

C. Assess what is actually needed given the project size and remaining complexity: a brief charter summary (even retroactive), documented scope agreement, and a high-level schedule provide minimum governance without bureaucratic overhead. Present these minimum viable artifacts to the sponsor as risk mitigation, not paperwork
D. Report the governance gaps to the PMO and wait for their instruction before taking any action
correct: C. Assess what is actually needed given the project size and remaining complexity: a brief charter summary (even retroactive), documented scope agreement, and a high-level schedule provide minimum viable governance without bureaucratic overhead. Present these minimum viable artifacts to the sponsor as risk mitigation, not paperwork
explanation: The sponsor's 'no paperwork' view reflects a legitimate frustration with over-documentation, not necessarily opposition to good practice. The PM should tailor: not enforce full PMI governance on a small project that has 70% remaining and has been functioning (somewhat), but also not leave the project without minimum viable governance. The tailored approach: a one-page charter summary that captures the project purpose and PM authority, a documented scope agreement that prevents scope disputes, and a high-level schedule for tracking. Frame these as risk mitigation tools — what happens when someone new joins, when a dispute arises, or when the sponsor's priorities shift? These risks justify minimum documentation. Adopting the 'no documentation' approach accepts unnecessary organizational risk.
source: PMBOK 7th Edition / Tailoring / PMP ECO Domain II Process / Initiation

question: An agile team's Product Owner has written 45 user stories for the next release. During a backlog refinement session, 18 stories have no acceptance criteria, 12 are estimated but too large to complete in one sprint, and 8 are dependent on an external API whose availability is uncertain. What should the team do before Sprint Planning?
options: A. Begin Sprint Planning — the refinement issues can be resolved during the sprint

B. Hold additional backlog refinement sessions: write acceptance criteria for the 18 stories, split the 12 oversized stories into sprint-sized items, and assess/document the API dependency risk for the 8 dependent stories — only stories meeting the Definition of Ready should enter Sprint Planning
C. Bring all 45 stories to Sprint Planning and let the team decide which are ready
D. Remove all stories that don't meet quality standards and ask the PO to rewrite them
correct: B. Hold additional backlog refinement sessions: write acceptance criteria for the 18 stories, split the 12 oversized stories into sprint-sized items, and assess/document the API dependency risk for the 8 dependent stories — only stories meeting the Definition of Ready should enter Sprint Planning
explanation: The Definition of Ready exists precisely to prevent Sprint Planning from becoming a requirements writing session — which consumes sprint time and produces lower-quality requirements than dedicated refinement. With 18 stories lacking acceptance criteria, 12 too large, and 8 with dependency uncertainty, very few of the 45 stories are ready for Sprint Planning. The team should: (1) Write acceptance criteria (PO collaborates with team), (2) Split oversized stories using established decomposition techniques, (3) Assess API dependency risk — is the API actually available? Spike needed? This work is the purpose of backlog refinement. Bringing unready stories to Sprint Planning spreads ambiguity into execution. Removing stories without collaboration eliminates PO agency.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Backlog Refinement / Definition of Ready

question: A PM is working in an organization where the culture strongly values hierarchy. The PM wants to introduce agile retrospectives, which require all team members including senior members to openly discuss what went wrong. A senior developer refuses to participate, saying 'this kind of meeting is beneath my level.' How should the PM respond?
options: A. Make retrospectives optional — the senior developer's discomfort is a cultural signal the PM should respect
B. Explain to the senior developer that retrospective participation is mandatory and address any further resistance through HR

C. Have a private conversation with the senior developer to understand their specific concern, explain the purpose and format of retrospectives, offer to adjust the format so their participation feels consistent with their professional level (e.g., opening reflection, focused technical improvement topics), and explore whether they might even facilitate a session to demonstrate their expertise
D. Conduct retrospectives without the senior developer and share summaries to keep them informed
correct: C. Have a private conversation with the senior developer to understand their specific concern, explain the purpose and format of retrospectives, offer to adjust the format so their participation feels consistent with their professional level (e.g., opening reflection, focused technical improvement topics), and explore whether they might even facilitate a session to demonstrate their expertise
explanation: The senior developer's resistance likely reflects the cultural discomfort of being put in an egalitarian format that their cultural schema interprets as status-reducing. Direct mandate (HR approach) will produce compliance without genuine participation — the least valuable retrospective outcome. The private conversation respects their status while creating space to address the actual concern. Reframing their role (technical expert sharing insights, facilitator demonstrating leadership) converts the format from perceived threat to opportunity. If they facilitate, they become retrospective champions. Exclusion from retrospectives means their technical insights — often the most valuable — are never captured, and they don't receive team feedback on their own contributions.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain I People T14 / Cultural Intelligence / Change Adoption

question: A project manager is conducting a Quantitative Risk Analysis using Monte Carlo simulation. The simulation runs 10,000 iterations and produces: P50 = Day 180, P80 = Day 195, P90 = Day 205. The project baseline is Day 175. A team member suggests the simulation is wrong because the team 'always delivers on time.' What is the most accurate response to this objection?
options: A. The team member may be right — Monte Carlo should be recalibrated against the team's historical performance

B. The Monte Carlo simulation reflects the inherent uncertainty in the input distributions (activity durations, probabilities), not any assumption about this team's historical performance. A baseline of Day 175 represents only the P5-P10 confidence level based on these results — achieving it requires either unusually favorable outcomes or corrective actions to shift the distribution
C. Discard the simulation results — qualitative expert judgment from the team supersedes statistical modeling
D. The team member is correct if they have a track record — past performance is the most reliable predictor
correct: B. The Monte Carlo simulation reflects the inherent uncertainty in the input distributions (activity durations, probabilities), not any assumption about this team's historical performance. A baseline of Day 175 represents only the P5-P10 confidence level based on these results — achieving it requires either unusually favorable outcomes or corrective actions to shift the distribution
explanation: The team member conflates 'we deliver on time' with 'the baseline we committed to is achievable.' Monte Carlo simulation produces a probability distribution based on the actual uncertainty ranges in estimates — it is not pessimistic, it is probabilistic. If the baseline sits at P5-P10 confidence, it means 90-95% of simulated outcomes show the project finishing AFTER the baseline. A team that 'always delivers on time' either: (1) consistently has generous baselines (which means they're not really delivering against plan), (2) takes extraordinary actions that compress the distribution in execution, or (3) their estimates contain implicit buffers not captured in the model. The simulation is revealing a risk the team's 'can-do' attitude may be hiding.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Monte Carlo Simulation / Quantitative Risk

question: A PM discovers that the organization's standard project reporting templates require reporting EVM metrics, but the project is using a pure Agile (Scrum) approach where EVM metrics are not naturally generated. The PMO requires template compliance. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: A. Convert all Agile metrics (velocity, burndown) to EVM equivalents and report both
B. Report only Agile metrics and decline the EVM requirement — Agile projects are incompatible with EVM

C. Engage with the PMO to discuss appropriate metrics for the Agile context: propose agile-native metrics (velocity trend, release burnup, sprint goal achievement rate) as equivalents that answer the same governance questions as EVM, while potentially maintaining a high-level EVM approximation (story points as 'value earned') for portfolio-level reporting continuity
D. Switch to a hybrid methodology to make EVM reporting technically feasible
correct: C. Engage with the PMO to discuss appropriate metrics for the Agile context: propose agile-native metrics (velocity trend, release burnup, sprint goal achievement rate) as equivalents that answer the same governance questions as EVM, while potentially maintaining a high-level EVM approximation (story points as 'value earned') for portfolio-level reporting continuity
explanation: PMO reporting requirements exist for governance reasons — the PM should understand what questions the EVM metrics are designed to answer and propose Agile-native equivalents that answer the same questions. Velocity trend answers 'are we performing efficiently?' — equivalent to CPI. Release burnup/burndown answers 'are we on track for the release?' — equivalent to SPI. Sprint goal achievement answers 'are we meeting commitments?' — equivalent to schedule performance. Some organizations do use story points as a proxy for EVM (story points earned vs. planned = EV/PV equivalent). The goal is governance continuity, not methodology compliance for its own sake. Switching methodology just to satisfy reporting requirements undermines the project's chosen approach.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Tailoring / Agile Metrics / PMO Governance

question: A project is entering closeout. The PM discovers that one vendor contract has a warranty clause requiring the vendor to provide support for 12 months post-delivery for any defects. Another vendor's contract expired when the project closed. During a post-implementation review 3 months later, significant defects are found. Which vendor is the organization's recourse against, and what is the PM's role?
options: A. Neither vendor — once the project is closed and deliverables accepted, vendor liability ends

B. The vendor with the active warranty clause may be held responsible for warranty-covered defects. The expired contract vendor has no remaining obligation. The PM should document the defect findings, identify which deliverables each vendor was responsible for, and work with legal/procurement to initiate warranty claims against the active-warranty vendor
C. Both vendors are equally liable — defect discovery within 12 months of delivery always triggers warranty
D. The PM has no role post-project — vendor issues are procurement's responsibility
correct: B. The vendor with the active warranty clause may be held responsible for warranty-covered defects. The expired contract vendor has no remaining obligation. The PM should document the defect findings, identify which deliverables each vendor was responsible for, and work with legal/procurement to initiate warranty claims against the active-warranty vendor
explanation: Vendor obligations are determined by contract terms — not by uniform rules. The warranty clause contract creates ongoing post-project obligation for the vendor to remediate covered defects during the warranty period. The expired contract creates no such ongoing obligation. The PM's role in post-project defect discovery: (1) Document the defects clearly (nature, severity, affected deliverable), (2) Trace each defect to the responsible vendor's deliverable, (3) Engage legal/procurement to initiate warranty claims through the appropriate contractual process. The PM serves as the technical context provider in this process — they know the project well enough to support the claim. Ignoring the issue and ceding entirely to procurement misses the PM's accountability for project outcomes.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process T11/T17 / Contract Administration / Post-Close

question: A PM is managing a critical path activity with a single person who has expert knowledge not available elsewhere. That person has become erratic — excellent work one week, completely disengaged the next. The team suspects personal issues. The deadline is 4 weeks away. What is the most effective management approach?
options: A. Performance-manage the individual — erratic delivery is a professional issue that must be addressed formally
B. Reassign the critical path work to reduce dependency on an unstable resource

C. Have a private, empathetic conversation to understand if there is a personal situation affecting performance; explore what support might help; make it clear the work is critical without adding pressure; simultaneously develop a contingency plan (cross-training, partial knowledge transfer, task decomposition) to reduce concentration risk — regardless of the personal situation outcome
D. Escalate to HR and let them handle the situation while the PM manages around the resource
correct: C. Have a private, empathetic conversation to understand if there is a personal situation affecting performance; explore what support might help; make it clear the work is critical without adding pressure; simultaneously develop a contingency plan (cross-training, partial knowledge transfer, task decomposition) to reduce concentration risk — regardless of the personal situation outcome
explanation: This requires parallel tracks: (1) The human track — a private, genuinely empathetic conversation. 'I've noticed some changes and want to check in — are you okay?' This serves two purposes: it's the right human thing to do, and it may reveal a resolvable situation (health issue, family emergency) that the PM or organization can actually help with. It should not add work pressure. (2) The project risk track — the PM cannot ignore that a single-point-of-failure expert is performing unpredictably with 4 weeks to deadline. Contingency planning (knowledge transfer, task decomposition, identifying backup skills) is responsible project management, independent of the personal situation. Formal performance management is premature and counterproductive if there's a genuine personal crisis. Reassignment without the human conversation is cold and may lose the person entirely.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain I People T3 / EQ / Risk Management / Team Wellbeing

question: A PM's project has 6 months of execution remaining. A PMO audit reveals the project has been using unapproved third-party libraries in the software build, violating the organization's approved technology list. The libraries are deeply integrated and removal would require significant rework. The development lead says the libraries were necessary for performance and were widely used. What is the required course of action?
options: A. The libraries are already integrated — retroactively add them to the approved list to comply technically

B. Document the unauthorized use, assess the risk and rework options, submit a change request to either formalize the library approval through the proper governance channel or plan for removal, and prevent any future unauthorized additions — without retroactively falsifying approval records
C. Remove the libraries immediately regardless of rework cost — policy violations must be remediated
D. Continue using the libraries but implement compensating controls to reduce the risk of violation consequences
correct: B. Document the unauthorized use, assess the risk and rework options, submit a change request to either formalize the library approval through the proper governance channel or plan for removal, and prevent any future unauthorized additions — without retroactively falsifying approval records
explanation: The PM must handle this with integrity — retroactively falsifying approval records is dishonest regardless of how it's framed. The correct sequence: (1) Document the violation transparently, (2) Assess options — can these libraries receive formal approval? (often possible for widely-used, legitimate libraries) What is the cost/risk of removal? (3) Submit to the appropriate governance process to formally approve or decline the libraries, (4) If approved through proper channels, the record shows the correct approval date, (5) If not approvable, plan compliant removal with appropriate change request. Immediate removal without analysis may be unnecessarily costly if approval is achievable. Continuing with compensating controls doesn't address the governance gap.
source: PMI Code of Ethics / PMP ECO Domain III BE T1 / Technical Governance

question: A PM is asked to estimate a new project. The organization has done 12 similar projects, but each took different amounts of time (range: 8-28 months, average: 16 months). The new project appears more complex than average. What estimation approach and communication of uncertainty is most appropriate?
options: A. Report 16 months — the historical average is the most defensible single estimate
B. Report 8 months — anchor on the best case to be competitive and manage upward from there

C. Use the historical range to inform a three-point estimate: assess this project's complexity relative to the historical projects, develop O/M/P estimates (O = best comparable, M = adjusted for this project's complexity, P = highest comparable + complexity factor), calculate PERT, and report the range with confidence levels rather than a single number — explicitly communicating that a definitive estimate requires more detailed planning
D. Decline to estimate until full requirements are available — any estimate without complete information is misleading
correct: C. Use the historical range to inform a three-point estimate: assess this project's complexity relative to the historical projects, develop O/M/P estimates (O = best comparable, M = adjusted for this project's complexity, P = highest comparable + complexity factor), calculate PERT, and report the range with confidence levels rather than a single number — explicitly communicating that a definitive estimate requires more detailed planning
explanation: Historical range (8-28 months) is itself valuable information — the variation tells us these projects are difficult to estimate precisely. For a project that is 'more complex than average,' the PM should: (1) Use the range to anchor O (best comparable = 8 months, maybe 12 for average complexity), M (average 16 months + complexity factor = perhaps 19), P (worst comparable = 28 months + complexity premium = 32). (2) PERT: (12 + 4×19 + 32)/6 = (12+76+32)/6 = 20 months with high uncertainty. (3) Report as '15-25 month range with 20 months as central estimate, pending detailed planning.' A single number from highly variable data implies false precision. Declining to estimate until requirements are complete typically means never estimating — organizations make decisions with available information.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Analogous Estimation / Three-Point PERT

question: A team is completing Sprint 12 of a planned 15-sprint project. The release burnup chart shows: planned scope = 300 points, completed = 240 points, and the scope line has increased from 300 to 340 points over the last 4 sprints due to newly discovered requirements. At current velocity (20 points/sprint), how many additional sprints are needed, and what conversation should the PM and PO have?
options: A. 3 more sprints — the original plan had 3 sprints remaining so the project is on track

B. 5 more sprints to complete 340 points at 20 points/sprint — but this is 8 sprints beyond the planned 15. The PM and PO must discuss: scope prioritization (can 40 new points be deprioritized to meet the original 15-sprint timeline?), release criteria (is 240/300 original scope deliverable now as a release?), or timeline extension (formally plan for 17 sprints with sponsor alignment)
C. The scope increase is expected in agile — continue at current velocity and report at 17 sprints
D. The project has failed scope management — all 40 new points must be removed from the backlog
correct: B. 5 more sprints to complete 340 points at 20 points/sprint — but this is 8 sprints beyond the planned 15. The PM and PO must discuss: scope prioritization (can 40 new points be deprioritized to meet the original 15-sprint timeline?), release criteria (is 240/300 original scope deliverable now as a release?), or timeline extension (formally plan for 17 sprints with sponsor alignment)
explanation: Burnup math: 340 total - 240 completed = 100 remaining. At 20 points/sprint: 100/20 = 5 more sprints = Sprint 17 total. This is 2 sprints beyond the original plan. The conversation the PM and PO must have is a trade-off analysis: (1) Can the 40 new scope points be ordered to the bottom of the backlog and deferred to the next release — restoring the 15-sprint plan? (2) Is the work completed so far releasable as a version 1.0, with remaining 60 original + 40 new points in a version 1.1? (3) Does the business need all 340 points and must the timeline extend? This is exactly what a burnup chart should surface — the scope increase is visible and enables proactive conversation rather than surprised schedule overrun.
source: PMP ECO Jan 2021 - Domain II Process / Release Burnup / Scope Management / Agile

question: A PM has just been asked to serve on the organization's PMO improvement committee while managing an active large project. The committee work will require approximately 8 hours/week over 3 months. The PM's current project has schedule pressure. PMO participation would develop the PM's skills and benefit the organization. What factors should guide the PM's decision, and what is the most professional approach?
options: A. Decline immediately — current project commitments must always take priority over additional responsibilities
B. Accept immediately — organizational development opportunities should never be declined

C. Assess the actual available capacity in the project schedule (not just current load, but projected over the 3-month period), consult with the project sponsor about the commitment and its organizational value, be honest about whether 8 hours/week is sustainable given project demands, and either accept with clear capacity management or decline with a specific future date when capacity will exist
D. Accept and plan to reduce project engagement slightly to accommodate both — trade-offs are normal in professional life
correct: C. Assess the actual available capacity in the project schedule (not just current load, but projected over the 3-month period), consult with the project sponsor about the commitment and its organizational value, be honest about whether 8 hours/week is sustainable given project demands, and either accept with clear capacity management or decline with a specific future date when capacity will exist
explanation: This is a professional judgment question that tests honest self-assessment and stakeholder transparency. The PM's first obligation is to the current project — taking on additional work that compromises it would be irresponsible. However, the correct process is not reflexive acceptance or refusal: (1) Honestly assess whether 8 hours/week is realistically available over the specific 3-month period (what phases is the project in? Are there crunch periods?), (2) Consult the project sponsor — they have a stake in the decision and may endorse or caution against the commitment, (3) Make a clear, honest decision and communicate it professionally. Reducing project engagement without acknowledgment is managing by attrition. The PM must not over-commit and under-deliver on either responsibility.
source: PMI Code of Ethics / PMP ECO Domain I People / Professional Responsibility
